author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the four chambers of the human heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessel systems entering and leaving cardiac tissue.
Trace the exact path of blood through both pulmonary and systemic loops of dual-circulation.
Differentiate the anatomical features of the right and left ventricles, explicitly linking muscle wall thickness to workload and arterial pressure.
Explain the passive, pressure-dependent operation of atrioventricular and semilunar valves during the cardiac cycle to prevent backward blood flow.

modules.description: An introduction to the external and internal structures of the human heart, aligning anatomical left and right orientation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand anatomical left/right reversal from the viewer's perspective.
Distinguish the intact external landmarks of the heart from its interior structural features.
instructions: Observe the orientation of the intact and cutaway heart models.
Rotate the models to inspect the relative position of the apex and base.

clips.changeMeaning: Initialize gross orientation labels and focus attention on the side-by-side heart models.
clips.narration: Welcome to the cardiovascular anatomy lab. Before us, we have two models of a human heart: on the left is the intact exterior view, and on the right is an interior cutaway view. Notice that the patient's right side is on your left, and the patient's left is on your right. This standard anatomical orientation is relative to the patient, not the viewer.

clips.changeMeaning: Orient both heart models dynamically to show the posterior side for context.
clips.narration: Take a moment to rotate the models. Notice how the major blood vessels connect to the upper base of the heart, while the muscular apex points downward and slightly to the patient's left.

modules.description: An interactive highlight tour of the four chambers, four valves, and five major blood vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Locate and name the four core heart chambers on a model.
Differentiate the anatomical locations and alternative names of cardiac valves (tricuspid, mitral/bicuspid, pulmonic, aortic).
Map internal chambers directly to external blood vessels.
instructions: Follow the yellow highlight pointer to trace critical heart chambers and valves.
Observe the text labels updating with the highlighted structures.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the pointer to highlight the Right Atrium.
clips.narration: Let's explore the four internal chambers of the heart. The pointer is highlighting the Right Atrium. This thin-walled receiving chamber collects deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circulation of the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the pointer to highlight the Right Ventricle.
clips.narration: Directly below the Right Atrium is the Right Ventricle. When the right atrium contracts, it pumps blood down into this chamber, which has muscular walls designed to push blood up into the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the pointer to highlight the Left Atrium.
clips.narration: On the opposite side, we find the Left Atrium. It receives highly oxygenated blood returning directly from the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the pointer to highlight the Left Ventricle.
clips.narration: Finally, blood flows down into the Left Ventricle. Notice its incredibly thick, muscular wall compared to the right ventricle. The left ventricle is the powerhouse of the heart, pumping oxygenated blood throughout the entire systemic loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the Tricuspid Valve situated between the RA and RV.
clips.narration: Now let's look at the four major valves that maintain one-way blood flow. First is the Tricuspid Valve, located between the right atrium and right ventricle. It prevents blood from flowing backward into the atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the Mitral (Bicuspid) Valve situated between the LA and LV.
clips.narration: On the left side, separating the left atrium and left ventricle, is the Mitral Valve, also commonly referred to as the Bicuspid Valve in clinical and anatomical contexts.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the Pulmonary and Aortic semilunar valves.
clips.narration: Lastly, we have the semilunar valves: the Pulmonary Valve guards the exit of the right ventricle, and the Aortic Valve guards the exit of the left ventricle. They prevent blood from draining back into the ventricles during relaxation.

modules.description: Visualization of oxygenated vs deoxygenated flow and the division of pulmonary vs systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish blue (deoxygenated) vs red (oxygenated) blood pathways.
Contrast the structural roles of the pulmonary and systemic circulatory circuits.
instructions: Examine the color-coded flow paths of the systemic and pulmonary loops.
Observe which parts of the heart host deoxygenated versus oxygenated blood.

clips.changeMeaning: Enable systemic and pulmonary visual circulation loops with distinct color cues.
clips.narration: The cardiovascular system relies on color-coded pathways to trace gas exchange. Oxygenated blood, rich in O2, is shown in bright red, while deoxygenated blood, returning from tissue metabolism, is depicted in blue. Let's look at how the heart keeps these circuits separated.

clips.changeMeaning: Dull systemic visualizer to focus solely on the pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: The right side of the heart drives the Pulmonary Circuit. Deoxygenated blue blood is pumped from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the lungs, where it expels CO2 and picks up O2, returning red to the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Shift visual highlighting back to systemic loop, pulling back on the pulmonary loop visual.
clips.narration: The left side drives the Systemic Circuit. Here, high-pressure, oxygenated red blood in the left ventricle is pumped into the aorta and distributed to capillary beds throughout the entire body to nourish active tissues.

modules.description: Step-by-step trace of a single red blood cell navigating the circulatory pathways.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the structural sequence of blood flow from body to lungs and back to body.
Explain where gas exchange occurs and its correlation with blood oxygenation colors.
instructions: Step through the stages of a single red blood cell's journey.
Watch how the cell swaps color from blue to red as it completes its loop through the lungs.

components.scriptDescription: A button component that lets students advance the RBC waypoint indices within a predefined coordinate array. Replaying the loop resets the RBC position.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the RBC at the Superior Vena Cava input.
clips.narration: Let's trace a single red blood cell through the entire loop. We begin in the Superior Vena Cava. The cell is deoxygenated, returning from upper body tissues, so it appears blue.

components.text: RBC Step 2: Right Atrium -> Tricuspid Valve

clips.changeMeaning: Move RBC into the Right Atrium.
clips.narration: The blood cell enters the Right Atrium, then passes through the open Tricuspid Valve downward into the right ventricle.

components.text: RBC Step 3: Right Ventricle -> Pulmonary Valve

clips.changeMeaning: Move RBC into the Right Ventricle.
clips.narration: In the Right Ventricle, pressure rises as it contracts. This snaps the tricuspid valve closed and pushes the cell through the Pulmonary Valve.

components.text: RBC Step 4: Pulmonary Arteries to Lungs (Oxygenation)

clips.changeMeaning: Move RBC to lungs and trigger color shift from blue to red.
clips.narration: The blood cell flows into the pulmonary trunk, traveling to the lung capillaries. Here, gas exchange occurs: CO2 is dumped, oxygen is loaded, and the cell changes from blue to a vibrant red.

components.text: RBC Step 5: Pulmonary Veins to Left Atrium

clips.changeMeaning: Move oxygenated RBC back to Left Atrium.
clips.narration: Returning via the pulmonary veins, the oxygen-rich cell enters the Left Atrium, sliding through the Mitral/Bicuspid valve into the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Move RBC into Left Ventricle and push through aortic valve out to systemic circulation.
clips.narration: The powerhouse Left Ventricle contracts forcefully, snapping the mitral valve shut and ejecting our red blood cell through the Aortic Valve into the vast Systemic Aorta to deliver oxygen to the body.

modules.description: Compare cross-sections of the right and left ventricles to examine muscular wall thickness differences.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate myocardial wall thickness to the vascular resistance of pulmonary vs systemic loops.
Recognize physical dimensions of healthy right vs left ventricle muscles.
instructions: Observe the cross-section slice of the heart.
Identify the thin-walled right ventricle and the thick, dominant left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Display ventricular cross-section highlighting structural wall thickness.
clips.narration: Why does the heart have such thickness asymmetry? Here is a cross-section showing both ventricles cut horizontally. On your left is the right ventricle, and on your right is the left ventricle. Notice the right ventricular wall is only about 3 to 5 millimeters thick.

clips.changeMeaning: Shift highlight focus to Left Ventricle wall.
clips.narration: Now look at the Left Ventricle wall: it measures 10 to 15 millimeters thick! This is a 3-to-1 ratio. Because the left ventricle must generate enough pressure to pump blood to the entire body against high peripheral resistance, it needs a significantly thicker muscle wall than the right side, which only pumps to the nearby lungs.

modules.description: Examine how atrioventricular and semilunar valves open and close to coordinate blood flow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast AV and semilunar valve behaviors during systolic contraction and diastolic relaxation.
Explain the mechanism by which pressure differences govern valve states.
instructions: Inspect the AV valve model on the left, and the Semilunar valve model on the right.
Observe how valve states swap during contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole).

clips.changeMeaning: Render valve mechanics with AV and SL valves in initial neutral state.
clips.narration: Heart valves operate purely on pressure gradients, preventing the backward flow of blood. Let's look at the two functional classes of valves: Atrioventricular, or AV valves, and Semilunar valves.

clips.changeMeaning: Switch valves to Systole state: AV closed, SL open.
clips.narration: During Systole (ventricular contraction), high pressure within the ventricles pushes the leaflets of the AV valves (Tricuspid and Mitral) upward until they snap shut, preventing backflow into the atria. Simultaneously, this pressure forces the Semilunar valves open, ejecting blood into the arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Switch valves to Diastole state: AV open, SL closed.
clips.narration: During Diastole (ventricular relaxation), ventricular pressure drops. The elastic recoil of the aorta and pulmonary trunks pushes blood backward, forcing the Semilunar flaps shut. At the same time, AV valves drop open to allow the ventricles to fill with blood from the atria.

modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Demonstrate accurate spatial localization of chambers, valves, and major vessels on a heart model.
instructions: Look at the highlighted area on the cutaway heart.
Tap the correct term on your quiz UI panel.

components.text: Structure ID Quiz: Locate the structures!

clips.changeMeaning: Prepare blank cutaway model for active anatomical testing.
clips.narration: Now it's time to test your knowledge. A structure on the cutaway heart will light up. Select the correct anatomical name on your floating menu. Good luck!

modules.description: Trace the logical flow path of blood through chambers, valves, and vessels in systemic and pulmonary circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Chronologically trace blood cell flow through the cardiac structures without errors.
Distinguish oxygenation conditions of specific vessels (e.g. pulmonary trunk vs systemic veins).
instructions: Read the prompt detailing the starting location of the blood cell.
Select the correct downstream anatomical structure from the multiple-choice interface.

components.scriptDescription: Runs sequential flow tracing simulation puzzles. Keeps track of state loops, registers downstream target structure selections from a list of options, and visualizes wrong turns.

components.text: Flow Tracing: What structure is next?

clips.changeMeaning: Set up tracing sequential questions.
clips.narration: Let's trace blood flow. If a unit of blood has just left the Right Ventricle, what structure does it enter next? Check your screen and select the correct step to complete the dual-circulation trace.

modules.description: A summarizing review of structural anatomy, systemic vs pulmonary loops, and valve mechanics.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Consolidate architectural, metabolic, and hemodynamic concepts of the cardiovascular system.
instructions: Review the consolidated summary items on the screen.
Interact with the rotating heart models to review landmarks before finishing.

components.text:
Lab Recap:
1. Chambers (RA, RV, LA, LV)
2. Valves (Tricuspid, Mitral, Semilunar)
3. Circuits (Pulmonary vs Systemic)
4. Asymmetry (LV Wall ~3x thicker)
5. Mechanics (AV/SL alternate states)

clips.changeMeaning: Display summary review board alongside spinning hearts.
clips.narration: Excellent work! You have completed the Human Heart lab. You can now identify the four chambers and four valves, trace blood through both the pulmonary and systemic loops, explain why the left ventricle's myocardium is three times thicker than the right, and understand how pressure manages the cardiac valves to keep blood flowing in one direction. Keep studying, and we will see you in the next lab!
